pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey on the Oise, founded 1129 as a daughter of Clairvaux; its infirmary hall survives and is known as the hall of the dead)
etymology: French ours, a bear, and camp, a field: the bear's field, from a local legend attached to the site.
biblical_def: Ourscamp was founded in 1129 beside the Oise in Picardy, a daughter of Clairvaux, and became a large and wealthy house. What survives is unusual: the roofless Gothic choir of the church stands as a shell, and beside it the thirteenth-century infirmary hall, long called the salle des morts — the hall of the dead — where the sick of the house were nursed and where they died. The building is intact and still in religious use. An abbey that kept a named room for dying in was doing something the modern world has arranged not to do, and Scripture is on the abbey's side. “And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27) is stated as a plain appointment; “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psa 90:12) makes the counting of them a prayer; and “LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am” (Psa 39:4) asks to be told. A house with a hall of the dead in daily view had its theology of mortality built into its floor plan.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infirmary as a lodging for the sick, a hospital; mortality as subjection to death or the necessity of dying, and also death; and die as to be deprived of respiration, of the circulation of blood, and other bodily functions.
webster_full: INFIRMARY, n. A lodging for the sick; a hospital, or place where the sick and infirm are received and nursed.
MORTALITY, n. Subjection to death, or the necessity of dying; also, death; and frequency of death.
DIE, v.i. To be deprived of respiration, of the circulation of blood, and other bodily functions, and rendered incapable of resuscitation.
FRAIL, a. Weak; infirm; liable to fail and decay; subject to casualties; easily destroyed.
NUMBER, v.t. To count; to reckon; to ascertain the units of any sum, collection or multitude.
scriptures: Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Psa 39:4
LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am.
Job 14:1
Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble.
corruption_summary: A Picardy abbey of 1129 whose surviving infirmary is still called the hall of the dead: a house with its theology of mortality built into the floor plan.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the numbering of days as a discipline. “that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psa 90:12) ties the counting to the wisdom — a man who will not think about dying will not think clearly about living either.

The live corruption is the modern management of death out of sight, into institutions designed so that most people never see it. That is a change in architecture before it is a change in doctrine, and it has made “Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble” (Job 14:1) sound like pessimism rather than observation. A hall of the dead at the heart of a house is the opposite arrangement, and the honester one.
roots_summary: Hebrew maveth (H4194), death; Hebrew yom (H3117), a day; Greek thanatos (G2288), death; Greek hapax (G530), once; Hebrew chadel (H2310), frail or transient.
roots_lines: Hebrew maveth (H4194) — death; in the Old Testament an enemy, never a friend.
Hebrew yom (H3117) — a day; “So teach us to number our days” (Psa 90:12).
Greek thanatos (G2288) — death; the last enemy, and a defeated one.
Greek hapax (G530) — once, once for all; “as it is appointed unto men once to die” (Heb 9:27).
Hebrew chadel (H2310) — frail, transient; “that I may know how frail I am” (Psa 39:4).
usage: “but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27) — the clause that makes the hall of the dead a serious room.
“the measure of my days, what it is” (Psa 39:4) — a prayer to be told the truth about oneself.
“is of few days, and full of trouble” (Job 14:1) — observation rather than gloom.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Aisne, founded 1134 as a daughter of Clairvaux and destroyed by artillery in 1917 on the Chemin des Dames)
etymology: French val clair, the bright valley — the same name as Clairvaux, given by its mother house; Latin vallis clara.
biblical_def: Vauclair was founded in 1134 on the slope below the Chemin des Dames in the Aisne, a daughter of Clairvaux bearing a French form of its mother's name. It survived the Revolution as ruins; it was obliterated in 1917, when the ridge above it became one of the worst battlefields of the First World War and the abbey was shelled flat. What stands today was excavated from the rubble after 1966. An abbey named the bright valley, reduced to foundations by artillery, is not a subject for easy moralising, and Scripture does not offer any. It offers instead a flat account of what men are: “From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?” (Jam 4:1), and a warning against reading each new catastrophe as the end: “And ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars: see that ye be not troubled: for all these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet” (Mat 24:6). The promise of an end to war is given, and it is given to God alone to keep: “He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder” (Psa 46:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines war as a contest between nations or states carried on by force; artillery as cannon, great guns, ordnance; and desolate as destitute or deprived of inhabitants, laid waste.
webster_full: WAR, n. A contest between nations or states, carried on by force, either for defense, or for revenging insults and redressing wrongs.
ARTILLERY, n. In a general sense, offensive weapons of war; but in present usage, cannon, great guns, or ordnance, with their furniture.
DESOLATE, a. Destitute or deprived of inhabitants; desert; uninhabited; laid waste; in a ruinous condition.
BATTLE, n. A fight or encounter between enemies, or opposing armies; an engagement.
RUBBISH, n. Fragments of buildings; broken or imperfect pieces of any structure; ruins.
scriptures: Jam 4:1
From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?
Mat 24:6
And ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars: see that ye be not troubled: for all these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet.
Psa 46:9
He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire.
Isa 2:4

And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
corruption_summary: A Clairvaux daughter of 1134 named the bright valley, shelled flat in 1917 on the Chemin des Dames and dug out of the rubble after 1966.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the diagnosis. James traces war to desire rather than to systems or accidents — “come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?” (Jam 4:1) — which is both more pessimistic and more hopeful than the usual accounts, since a disease correctly named can be treated.

The second thing to say is that the promise of beaten swords is eschatological and not political. “nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more” (Isa 2:4) follows the judging of the nations by God himself; no treaty has delivered it, and a Christian who expects one is reading the passage as a programme rather than a prophecy.

roots_lines: Latin vallis clara — bright valley; the same name as Clairvaux, in French dress.
Hebrew milchamah (H4421) — war, battle; “neither shall they learn war any more” (Isa 2:4).
Hebrew cherev (H2719) — a sword; “he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder” (Psa 46:9).
Greek polemos (G4171) — war; “ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars” (Mat 24:6).
Greek hedone (G2237) — pleasure, desire; the root James assigns to war.

“see that ye be not troubled” (Mat 24:6) — a command against reading every war as the last.
“He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth” (Psa 46:9) — the promise, and whose it is to keep.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Thierache of Picardy, founded 1121 as an early daughter of Clairvaux)
etymology: From the locality in the Thiérache; a French place name of uncertain derivation, probably from a wooded or beech-growing ground.
biblical_def: Foigny was founded in 1121 in the wooded Thiérache, among the earliest daughters of Clairvaux, settled when Bernard's own house was four years old and already sending out colonies. Its church became one of the largest Cistercian buildings in France; practically nothing of it remains, the site having been quarried and farmed. The interest of Foigny is its place in the sequence: it belongs to the first wave, the years when the Cistercian movement was plainly a work of God in the judgment of everyone who saw it, before wealth and privilege complicated the account. Scripture has a word for a first instalment that guarantees the rest, and it uses it of Christ and of the Spirit rather than of institutions: “But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept” (1Co 15:20), and “For if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy: and if the root be holy, so are the branches” (Rom 11:16). A first daughter house guarantees nothing; the Cistercian first wave was followed by a long second one in which the same constitution produced very different men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines firstfruits as the fruits or produce first matured and collected in any season, offered to God, and figuratively the first profits or effects of any thing; and colony as a company of people transplanted from their mother country.
webster_full: FIRSTFRUITS, n. The fruits or produce first matured and collected in any season. These, among the Israelites, were offered to God.
FIRSTFRUITS, n. The first profits of any thing; also, the first or earliest effect of any thing, in a good or bad sense.
COLONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country.
DAUGHTER, n. The female offspring of a man or woman; a female descendant in any degree.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis or lowest part of an edifice; also, the act of founding; endowment; a donation or legacy appropriated to support an institution.
scriptures: But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.
For if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy: and if the root be holy, so are the branches.
Rev 2:4
Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love.
Gal 3:3
Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?
corruption_summary: An early Clairvaux daughter of 1121, now almost wholly gone: a first-wave house, from the years before privilege complicated the Cistercian account.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that first love is not self-sustaining. “Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love” (Rev 2:4) is written to a church that had kept its doctrine and its labour, which is exactly the Cistercian story in miniature.

The live warning is for reform movements generally. “Are ye so foolish? having begun in the Spirit, are ye now made perfect by the flesh?” (Gal 3:3) is Paul's question to converts drifting into works, and it applies to any movement that begins in genuine devotion and ends in a system. Foigny began well, built enormously, and left a field.
roots_summary: Hebrew bikkurim (H1061), firstfruits; Hebrew reshith (H7225), the beginning; Greek aparche (G536), firstfruits; Greek protos (G4413), first; Greek agape (G26), love.
roots_lines: Hebrew bikkurim (H1061) — firstfruits, the earliest ripe produce brought to God.
Hebrew reshith (H7225) — a beginning, the first of a thing; the word of Genesis 1:1.
Greek aparche (G536) — firstfruits; “become the firstfruits of them that slept” (1Co 15:20).
Greek agape (G26) — love; “thou hast left thy first love” (Rev 2:4).
Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; “are ye now made perfect by the flesh?” (Gal 3:3).
usage: “But now is Christ risen from the dead” (1Co 15:20) — the only firstfruit that guarantees the harvest.
“because thou hast left thy first love” (Rev 2:4) — the fate of a first-wave movement.
“having begun in the Spirit” (Gal 3:3) — the question every reform must keep answering.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Champagne, founded 1118 as the first daughter of Clairvaux; the three fountains)
etymology: French trois fontaines, three fountains or springs, from Latin tres fontes; named for the springs of the site.
biblical_def: Trois-Fontaines in Champagne was the first daughter of Clairvaux, settled in 1118 within a year of Bernard's arrival at the mother house, and it is therefore the beginning of the filiation that would eventually cover Europe. Its medieval buildings were largely replaced in the eighteenth century and ruined after the Revolution; a great gateway and fragments stand. The name is the entry's substance, because springs are the Cistercian obsession in their choice of sites and the Bible's great image for God himself. The three fountains of a Champagne valley are a good occasion to set out the biblical ones. “For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light” (Psa 36:9); “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13); and Christ's own promise, “the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (Joh 4:14). Jeremiah's contrast is the one to keep: a spring is given and a cistern is dug, and men prefer the cistern because they made it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fountain as a spring or source of water, the head of a stream, and figuratively the source or first principle of any thing; cistern as an artificial reservoir for holding water; and spring as a fountain of water, an issue of water from the earth.
webster_full: FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; properly, a spring or issuing of water from the earth; also, the head or source of a stream.
FOUNTAIN, n. Original; first principle or cause; the source of any thing.
CISTERN, n. An artificial reservoir or receptacle for holding water, beer or other liquor.
SPRING, n. A fountain of water; an issue of water from the earth, or the basin of water at the place of its issue.
WELL, n. A spring; a fountain; also, a pit or cylindrical hole sunk into the earth to the water.
scriptures: Psa 36:9
For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light.
Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
Joh 4:14
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
Rev 21:6
And he said unto me, It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely.
corruption_summary: The first daughter of Clairvaux, founded 1118, named for its springs: a good place to set out Jeremiah's contrast between a given fountain and a dug cistern.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Jeremiah names is the deepest one in religion and it is not confined to Rome. Men forsake a living spring and dig their own tank, because a tank is theirs: “For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13). Vows, austerities, relics, indulgences — and on the Protestant side, programmes, experiences and techniques — are all cisterns, and the verse ends by noting that they leak.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the freeness of the fountain. “I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely” (Rev 21:6) is the last word of the Bible on the subject, and the operative word is the last one.
roots_summary: Hebrew maqor (H4726), a fountain or source; Hebrew bor (H877), a cistern; Hebrew mayim chayyim, living water; Greek pege (G4077), a spring; Greek dorean (G1432), freely.
roots_lines: Hebrew maqor (H4726) — a fountain, a source; “with thee is the fountain of life” (Psa 36:9).
Hebrew bor (H877) — a pit or cistern; “broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13).
Greek pege (G4077) — a spring, well; “a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (Joh 4:14).
Greek dorean (G1432) — freely, as a gift; “of the fountain of the water of life freely” (Rev 21:6).
Latin tres fontes — three fountains; the abbey's own name.
usage: “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters” (Jer 2:13) — the first of the two evils.
“in thy light shall we see light” (Psa 36:9) — the fountain that is a person.
“shall never thirst” (Joh 4:14) — what a spring does that a cistern cannot.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Haute-Marne, founded 1135 as a daughter of Clairvaux; its buildings served as a prison in the nineteenth century)
etymology: From Latin alba ripa, the white bank, through Old French; named for the pale bank of the Aube valley.
biblical_def: Auberive was founded in 1135 in the upper Aube valley of Champagne, a daughter of Clairvaux, and rebuilt in the eighteenth century. Sold at the Revolution, its ranges were converted in the nineteenth century into a house of detention — first for political prisoners, later a women's prison and reformatory — and the cloister that had been built for monks held inmates for decades. The reversal is worth more than irony, because the care of prisoners is a duty Scripture lays on the church in the plainest terms. “I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Mat 25:36) sets Christ himself in the cell; “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body” (Heb 13:3) asks for identification and not merely charity; and the messianic commission includes release: “he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound” (Isa 61:1). An abbey that became a prison was given, late and unintentionally, a mission field at its own address.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prison as a public building for the confinement of debtors and criminals; captive as a prisoner taken by force or stratagem; and bonds as chains, fetters, that which confines or restrains.
webster_full: PRISON, n. A public building for the confinement or safe custody of debtors and criminals committed by process of law; a jail.
CAPTIVE, n. A prisoner taken by force or stratagem in war, by an enemy; also, one who is charmed or subdued.
BOND, n. Any thing that binds, as a cord, a chain, a rope; a band; in the plural, chains; imprisonment; captivity.
DETENTION, n. The act of detaining; a keeping back; a withholding; confinement; restraint.
LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint, in a general sense; natural liberty, civil liberty, political liberty, spiritual liberty.
scriptures: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
Isa 61:1

The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
Luk 4:18

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,
corruption_summary: A Clairvaux daughter of 1135 whose cloister became a nineteenth-century prison: a mission field delivered, late and unintentionally, to its own address.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is prison visiting as an unavoidable Christian duty. “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3) is not satisfied by sympathy at a distance, and the great majority of congregations do nothing about it at all.

The second thing to notice is the scope of the messianic commission, which includes the cell by name: “to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised” (Luk 4:18). Christ read that passage in a synagogue and said it was fulfilled in him. A church that reads it as metaphor only has cut out half of what he claimed.

Hebrew asir (H616) — a prisoner, one bound; the Psalter's word for those God hears.
Hebrew shebi (H7628) — captivity; “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Isa 61:1).
Greek desmos (G1199) — a bond, fetter; “Remember them that are in bonds” (Heb 13:3).
Greek aphesis (G859) — release, remission; “to preach deliverance to the captives” (Luk 4:18).

“as being yourselves also in the body” (Heb 13:3) — identification, not distant pity.
“the opening of the prison to them that are bound” (Isa 61:1) — part of the commission Christ claimed.

pos: n. (the name of several Cistercian houses, chiefly a daughter of Clairvaux in the Franche-Comte and a Cistercian nunnery in the Ardennes; the clear spring)
etymology: French claire fontaine, clear spring, from Latin clara fons; one of the commonest Cistercian names.
biblical_def: Clairefontaine is borne by several Cistercian foundations — a house of monks in the Franche-Comté in the Clairvaux line, and a nunnery in the Ardennes with a traditional connection to the counts of Luxembourg — and the repetition is the point. The order named its houses over and over for clear water: Clairvaux, Clairefontaine, Fontfroide, Trois-Fontaines, Fontenay, Beaufont. A Cistercian site had to have a stream, both because a drained marsh and a working mill need one and because the founders meant the name to preach. What they meant by it, Scripture says better. “For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light” (Psa 36:9) makes God the spring; “And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Rev 22:1) gives the clearest water in the Bible a source and a destination; and “He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (Joh 7:38) makes the believer a conduit rather than a reservoir.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines clear as open, free from obstruction, also bright, luminous, transparent; fountain as a spring or source of water; and pure as separate from all heterogeneous or extraneous matter, clear, free from mixture.
webster_full: CLEAR, a. Open; free from obstruction; also, bright; luminous; transparent; as clear water; a clear sky.
FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; properly, a spring or issuing of water from the earth.
PURE, a. Separate from all heterogeneous or extraneous matter; clear; free from mixture; as pure water.
CRYSTAL, a. Consisting of crystal, or like crystal; clear; pellucid; transparent.
RIVER, n. A large stream of water flowing in a channel on land into the ocean, a lake or another river.
scriptures: Psa 36:9
For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light.
Rev 22:1
And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.
Joh 7:38
He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.
O LORD, the hope of Israel, all that forsake thee shall be ashamed, and they that depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living waters.
corruption_summary: A name borne by several Cistercian houses, the clear spring: the order named its sites again and again for water it meant to preach from.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer is a channel and not a tank. “out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (Joh 7:38) describes outflow, and a Christian whose religion is entirely a matter of personal supply has mistaken himself for a cistern.

The live warning is Jeremiah's again, in its sharper form: “all that forsake thee shall be ashamed, and they that depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the LORD, the fountain of living waters” (Jer 17:13). A clear spring is a gift and not an achievement, and a house named for one can still run dry in every sense but the hydrological.
roots_summary: Latin clara fons, clear spring; Hebrew ayin (H5869), a spring or eye; Hebrew nahar (H5104), a river; Greek potamos (G4215), a river; Greek katharos (G2513), pure.
roots_lines: Latin clara fons — clear spring; one of the order's favourite names.
Hebrew ayin (H5869) — a spring, and also an eye; Hebrew sees a spring as the land's eye.
Hebrew nahar (H5104) — a river, a flowing stream; the rivers of Eden and of the prophets.
Greek potamos (G4215) — a river; “rivers of living water” (Joh 7:38).
Greek katharos (G2513) — pure, clean; “a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal” (Rev 22:1).
usage: “proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Rev 22:1) — the source of the clearest water in Scripture.
“He that believeth on me” (Joh 7:38) — the condition of being a channel.
“the fountain of living waters” (Jer 17:13) — the spring a man may still forsake.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Marne, founded 1127 as a daughter of Clairvaux, where William of Saint-Thierry went to live as a simple monk)
etymology: From the locality in the Marne near Reims; a French place name of uncertain derivation.
biblical_def: Igny was founded in 1127 in the Marne near Reims, a daughter of Clairvaux, and it has one claim that outweighs its buildings. William of Saint-Thierry, a Benedictine abbot, a theologian and Bernard's friend, resigned his abbacy in 1135 and came to Igny to be an ordinary Cistercian monk, afterwards going on to Signy. A man of standing laying down office to be nobody in particular is a rare thing in any century, and Scripture commends the disposition without qualification. “Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child” (Psa 131:2) is the inner state; “Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit” (Ecc 4:6) is the calculation; and “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) is the apostolic instruction that most ambitious Christians have never taken seriously. The house was destroyed in the First World War and rebuilt; it is a Trappist community of women today.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines quiet as rest, repose, stillness, freedom from alarm or disturbance; resign as to give up, to relinquish, as to resign an office; and humility as freedom from pride and arrogance, a modest estimate of one's own worth.
webster_full: QUIET, n. Rest; repose; stillness; the state of a thing not in motion; also, freedom from alarm or disturbance; peace; security.
RESIGN, v.t. To give up; to relinquish; as, to resign a claim or pretension; to resign an office.
HUMILITY, n. In ethics, freedom from pride and arrogance; humbleness of mind; a modest estimate of one's own worth.
RETIRE, v.i. To withdraw; to retreat; to go from company or from a public station into privacy.
WEAN, v.t. To accustom and reconcile, as a child or other young animal, to a want or deprivation of the breast.
scriptures: Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child.
Ecc 4:6
Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit.
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
Phi 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
corruption_summary: A Clairvaux daughter of 1127 where William of Saint-Thierry resigned an abbacy to be an ordinary monk: a rare laying down of office, and a disposition Scripture commends without reserve.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the weaned soul. “my soul is even as a weaned child” (Psa 131:2) describes a man who has stopped demanding, and it is the hardest short psalm in the Psalter to say honestly.

The live corruption is the Christian career: ministry as a ladder, with the platform at the top and the quiet work at the bottom. Paul inverts it — “Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves” (Phi 2:3) — and “that ye study to be quiet” (1Th 4:11) makes obscurity something to aim at rather than endure.
roots_summary: Greek hesuchazo (G2270), to be quiet; Hebrew damam (H1826), to be still; Hebrew gamal (H1580), to wean; Greek tapeinophrosune (G5012), lowliness of mind; Hebrew nachath (H5183), quietness.
roots_lines: Hebrew gamal (H1580) — to wean, to deal fully with; “as a child that is weaned of his mother” (Psa 131:2).
Hebrew nachath (H5183) — quietness, rest; “Better is an handful with quietness” (Ecc 4:6).
Greek hesuchazo (G2270) — to be still, to live quietly; “that ye study to be quiet” (1Th 4:11).
Greek tapeinophrosune (G5012) — lowliness of mind; “in lowliness of mind” (Phi 2:3).
Hebrew damam (H1826) — to be silent, to rest; the Psalter's stillness before God.
usage: “than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit” (Ecc 4:6) — the calculation behind a resignation.
“Surely I have behaved and quieted myself” (Psa 131:2) — the state, hard to claim honestly.
“and to do your own business” (1Th 4:11) — obscurity as an apostolic aim.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Ardennes, founded in the 1130s, where William of Saint-Thierry was abbot and died)
etymology: From the locality in the Ardennes, Signy-l'Abbaye; a French place name, the village taking the abbey's name after it.
biblical_def: Signy in the Ardennes was founded in the 1130s in the Clairvaux filiation, and William of Saint-Thierry — who had resigned a Benedictine abbacy to become a Cistercian at Igny — became its abbot and died there about 1148. His best work was written at Signy, including the Epistola ad fratres de Monte Dei, the golden letter to the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu, and a treatise on the nature and dignity of love. A man who gave up office, took it again in a poorer house, and spent his last years writing on the love of God has a claim on Protestant attention whatever one makes of his monasticism. The text for such a life is Paul's own summing up: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7). Nothing of the abbey's church remains; the village of Signy-l'Abbaye keeps its name, which is the usual arrangement in France — the stones go and the toponym stays.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines course as a passing, a moving, the progress of any thing, also the ground run or passed over; finish as to arrive at the end of, to bring to an end; and faith as the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another.
webster_full: COURSE, n. A passing; a moving, or motion forward; the ground, way or path run or passed over; also, the progress of any thing; manner of proceeding.
FINISH, v.t. To arrive at the end of, in a literal sense; to complete; to bring to an end; to perfect.
FAITH, n. The assent of the mind or understanding to the truth of what God has revealed; also, evangelical, justifying, or saving faith.
FIGHT, n. A battle; an engagement; a contest in arms; also, a struggle or contention of any kind.
ABBOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
scriptures: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
corruption_summary: An Ardennes abbey where William of Saint-Thierry was abbot and died: a man who laid down office, took it again in a poorer house, and wrote on the love of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the finishing of a course. “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing” (2Ti 4:8) extends Paul's confidence to every believer and withholds it from nobody who loves Christ's return.

The live corruption is unfinished Christianity: enthusiasm at the start, a long middle, and no account taken of the end. Paul kept the end in view and ran accordingly — “so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus” (Act 20:24), and “So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24).
roots_summary: Greek dromos (G1408), a course or race; Greek agon (G73), a contest; Greek teleo (G5055), to finish; Greek stephanos (G4735), a crown; Greek pistis (G4102), faith.
roots_lines: Greek dromos (G1408) — a running course; “I have finished my course” (2Ti 4:7).
Greek agon (G73) — a contest, a fight; the noun behind Paul's good fight.
Greek teleo (G5055) — to finish, complete; the verb of a life brought to its end.
Greek stephanos (G4735) — a victor's wreath; “a crown of righteousness” (2Ti 4:8).
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith; “I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7).
usage: “I have fought a good fight” (2Ti 4:7) — the text for a finished life.
“that I might finish my course with joy” (Act 20:24) — the end kept in view throughout.
“So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24) — the manner of running that reaches it.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Belgian Ardennes, Cistercian from 1132 and Trappist today, known for its brewery; the golden valley)
etymology: French or val, the valley of gold, from Latin aurea vallis; a local legend attaches the name to a countess's ring recovered from the spring.
biblical_def: Orval lies in the Belgian Ardennes, a community of Italian monks from about 1070 which joined the Cistercians in 1132 and, after destruction in 1793 and a long abandonment, was refounded in 1926 as a Trappist abbey. It is best known outside Belgium for its brewery, whose profits support the community and local charity. The name means the golden valley, from a story about a countess who lost a ring in the spring and had it returned by a trout. The brewery makes this entry a useful place to state the biblical position on drink, which is neither of the positions commonly taken. Wine is a good gift — “And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man's heart” (Psa 104:15) — and “For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4) forbids calling it unclean. Drunkenness is just as plainly condemned: “Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise” (Pro 20:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brewery as a brewhouse, the house and apparatus where brewing is carried on; temperance as moderation, particularly habitual moderation in regard to the indulgence of the appetites; and drunkenness as intoxication, inebriation.
webster_full: BREWERY, n. A brewhouse; the house and apparatus where brewing is carried on.
BREW, v.t. To boil or seethe; to make beer or ale from malt and other ingredients.
TEMPERANCE, n. Moderation; particularly, habitual moderation in regard to the indulgence of the natural appetites and passions.
DRUNKENNESS, n. Intoxication; inebriation; a state in which a person is overwhelmed or overpowered with spirituous liquors.
MODERATION, n. The state of being moderate, or of keeping a due mean between extremes or excess of violence.
scriptures: And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man's heart.
For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:
Pro 20:1
Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.
Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
corruption_summary: A Trappist abbey in the Belgian Ardennes whose brewery supports it: a useful place to state that Scripture calls wine a gift and drunkenness a sin, and will not let either swallow the other.
corruption_paragraphs: There are two corruptions here and they are mirror images. The first is licence, and Scripture condemns it without softening: “And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18), and the woe of “Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink” (Isa 5:11). Worse is to make another man drunk: “Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that puttest thy bottle to him, and makest him drunken also” (Hab 2:15).

The second corruption is the prohibitionist one, which calls a creature of God unclean and so adds to Scripture. “For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4) settles the question of the thing itself, and Paul prescribed wine medicinally to Timothy. The principle to recover is temperance, which is harder than either abstinence or indulgence: “Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God” (1Co 10:31).
roots_summary: Latin aurea vallis, golden valley; Hebrew yayin (H3196), wine; Hebrew shekar (H7941), strong drink; Greek oinos (G3631), wine; Greek nephalios (G3524), sober.
roots_lines: Latin aurea vallis — the golden valley; the abbey's name and its ring legend.
Hebrew yayin (H3196) — wine; “wine that maketh glad the heart of man” (Psa 104:15).
Hebrew shekar (H7941) — strong drink; “strong drink is raging” (Pro 20:1).
Greek oinos (G3631) — wine; “And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess” (Eph 5:18).
Greek nephalios (G3524) — sober, temperate; a qualification Paul requires of elders and deacons.
usage: “and bread which strengtheneth man's heart” (Psa 104:15) — wine listed among God's plain provisions.
“whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise” (Pro 20:1) — the other half, stated as plainly.
“do all to the glory of God” (1Co 10:31) — the rule that governs both the cup and the refusal of it.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Brabant, founded 1146 by monks sent from Clairvaux; now one of the largest monastic ruins in Europe)
etymology: French villers, from Latin villare, a hamlet or farm settlement, with la ville, the town; the farm settlement that became a town.
biblical_def: Villers in Brabant was founded in 1146 by a party Bernard sent from Clairvaux, and grew into one of the greatest abbeys of the Low Countries, with a vast church, immense ranges and estates across Brabant. Suppressed in 1796, quarried, cut through by a railway and left to the woods, it is now among the largest and most photographed monastic ruins in Europe — a hundred metres of roofless nave with trees growing in the triforium. The ruin is the entry, and Scripture has a register for it that is neither triumph nor sentiment but lament. “Our holy and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burned up with fire: and all our pleasant things are laid waste” (Isa 64:11) is a prayer, not a gloat; “How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!” (Lam 1:1) teaches a people how to grieve over what their own sin brought down. A Protestant looking at Villers may hold that its theology was wrong and still say those words over it, and he will be the better for doing so.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ruin as the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work of men; lamentation as expression of sorrow, cries of grief; and waste as desolate, destroyed, ruined.
webster_full: RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; also, in the plural, the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work of men.
LAMENTATION, n. Expression of sorrow; cries of grief; the act of bewailing.
WASTE, a. Destroyed; ruined; desolate; stripped; as, the land is laid waste.
DESOLATION, n. The act of deserting or abandoning; destruction; a desolate state; gloominess; sadness.
MAGNIFICENT, a. Grand in appearance; splendid; pompous; displaying grandeur.
scriptures: Our holy and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burned up with fire: and all our pleasant things are laid waste.
Lam 1:1
How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!
Psa 74:7
They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.
They shall perish, but thou shalt endure: yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed:
corruption_summary: A great Brabant abbey of 1146, now among the largest monastic ruins in Europe: a ruin Scripture teaches us to lament rather than enjoy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lament. “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name” (Psa 74:7) is a psalm, which means God has given his people words for exactly this grief; and a Protestant who feels only vindication at a wrecked abbey has a harder heart than the Psalmist.

The live misuse is the romantic one — the ruin as scenery, photographed for its atmosphere by people with no interest in what it was for. That is its own kind of forgetting. “They shall perish, but thou shalt endure” (Psa 102:26) is the only comfort on offer, and it is addressed to God rather than to the building.
roots_summary: Latin villare, a farm settlement; Hebrew shamem (H8074), to be desolate; Hebrew chorbah (H2723), a waste place; Greek eremosis (G2050), desolation; Hebrew qinah (H7015), a lamentation.
roots_lines: Latin villare — a hamlet or farmstead; the commonest place-name element in northern France and Belgium.
Hebrew shamem (H8074) — to be desolate, stunned; the word carries both the ruin and the horror at it.
Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a waste, a ruin; “all our pleasant things are laid waste” (Isa 64:11).
Hebrew qinah (H7015) — a dirge, lamentation; the form of the book of Lamentations.
Greek eremosis (G2050) — desolation; the New Testament's word for a sanctuary laid waste.
usage: “where our fathers praised thee” (Isa 64:11) — a prayer over a wrecked sanctuary.
“how is she become as a widow!” (Lam 1:1) — grief taught to a people by God himself.
“They shall perish, but thou shalt endure” (Psa 102:26) — the only durable comfort before a ruin.
